What is the essential teaching in 'In the Context of the Deathless'?

In 'In the Context of the Deathless', the teaching opens with this observation: *"For a long time, especially in the West, the Buddha has had a reputation for being a pessimist, and the passage we chanted just now would seem to confirm that reputation."* The central invitation is to turn one's investigation inward — to verify the Dhamma not as a set of beliefs, but as directly observable reality in one's own body, speech, and mind. As the text teaches, the Dhamma is *akāliko* — ever-present — and *opanayiko* — leading inward — available to be known (*paccattaṁ*) by each practitioner for themselves. There is no need to search elsewhere; the truth is already here.

Why does 'In the Context of the Deathless' place such emphasis on contemplating the body?

The text teaches: *"For a long time, especially in the West, the Buddha has had a reputation for being a pessimist, and the passage we chanted just now would seem to confirm that reputation. The world is swept away. It does not endure. It offers no shelter. There’s no one in charge. You have nothing of your own. You ha..."* Body contemplation (kāyagatāsati) is the Buddha's own recommended entry point because the body is always with us and plainly reveals the three characteristics: it is impermanent (anicca), involves stress (dukkha), and is not a self (anattā). Beginning with the five meditation themes — hair of head, hair of body, nails, teeth, skin — the practitioner trains the eye of discernment (paññā) to see through the illusion of beauty and find the inherent truth beneath. Right now, bring gentle attention to the feel of your body sitting — notice it is always changing.
